target.title: Learning from the Master: Distilling Cross-modal Advanced Knowledge for Lip Reading

read.pdf: Fig. 1-2 and Tables 1-6 (figure captions and table text read)

entries.text: The proposed framework replaces a fixed pretrained teacher with a trainable master network.
entries.condition: Training framework for silent-video lip reading; the master receives audio and video.
entries.quote: Instead of us- ing a pretrained teacher network, we design a trainable and much more powerful network named “master”.

entries.text: The master emits logits from audio-only, video-only, and combined audio-visual features.
entries.condition: The three streams are outputs of the trainable master.

entries.text: Student feedback is used to adapt the master's teaching content to the student's task-specific needs.
entries.condition: During the master-training stage, a temporarily updated student supplies feedback; the main student parameters are fixed.
entries.quote: The master could be adjusted according to the feedback of the student, and thus provides bi- modal knowledge dynamically for the student to learn in a better way.

entries.text: Audio and video tutor networks guide the fusion of knowledge from the two modalities.
entries.condition: Tutors are pretrained; their backend features determine modality weights, rather than directly transferring tutor logits to the student.

entries.text: A curriculum ranks samples by tutor confidence and increases the included training fraction with an exponential pacing schedule.
entries.condition: Training data are ranked using audio- and video-tutor confidence; equal ratings are re-sorted by video confidence.
entries.quote: By measuring and sorting the difﬁculty of samples, it could enhance the effectiveness of model training as well as ensuring a better convergence.

entries.text: The authors claim state-of-the-art results on the three evaluated word- and sentence-level benchmarks.
entries.condition: LRW, LRS2-BBC, and LRS3-TED; WER comparisons in Table 2.

entries.text: The student takes video as input; the master receives both audio and video during training.
entries.condition: Audio is available to the training-time master and audio tutor; student input is visual. The paper does not present a separate deployment study.

entries.text: Video inputs are sampled at 25 frames per second and processed into lip-centered 112×112 images.
entries.condition: Visual preprocessing: dlib facial landmarks, random crop and interpolation, then face rotation/scale transformation.

entries.text: Lip-centered inputs are 112×112; faces are landmark-aligned, randomly cropped/interpolated, and transformed to remove rotation and scale differences.
entries.condition: Preprocessing for benchmark videos; landmark detector cited as dlib [5].

entries.text: Word-level output uses a 500-word vocabulary; sentence-level output uses a 40-symbol vocabulary consisting of letters, digits, and special tokens.
entries.condition: LRW word prediction; LRS2-BBC and LRS3-TED character-by-character sentence prediction.

entries.text: The evaluation uses LRW for word-level recognition and LRS2-BBC and LRS3-TED for sentence-level recognition.
entries.condition: LRW is word-level; LRS2-BBC and LRS3-TED are sentence-level audiovisual datasets.

entries.text: LRW is described as a 500-word dataset with 450,000 utterances.
entries.condition: Dataset-level LRW description, not the evaluation-subset size.

entries.text: The dataset is split into pretrain, train-val, and test data; train-val and pretrain come from the same date, and pretrain contains word-level boundary alignment.
entries.condition: The paper does not give the exact split sizes or split-construction details in this description.

entries.text: WER is the metric for all experiments, computed from substitutions, deletions, and insertions divided by reference-word count.
entries.condition: S, D, and I are substitution, deletion, and insertion counts; NUM is the number of words in the reference.

entries.text: The introduction says the lip-reading versus speech-recognition WER gap can reach 40%.
entries.condition: Prior-work contextual claim cited to [1]; the sentence does not name a specific evaluation partition.

entries.text: Table 1 reports LRS2-BBC lip-reading WER of 57.5.
entries.condition: LRS2-BBC; same teacher/student structures except for teacher modality as described in Sec. 1; exact test partition is not specified alongside the table.
entries.quote: Lip reading % - 57.5

entries.text: Table 2 reports WAS WER of 23.8 on LRW and 70.4 on LRS2-BBC.
entries.condition: LRW word-level and LRS2-BBC sentence-level benchmarks; outside-method results are copied from original papers unless otherwise stated.

entries.text: Table 2 reports TM-CTC WER of 65.0 on LRS2-BBC and 74.7 on LRS3-TED.
entries.condition: LRS2-BBC and LRS3-TED sentence-level benchmarks; outside-method results are copied from original papers unless otherwise stated.

entries.text: Table 2 reports TM-Seq2Seq WER of 49.8 on LRS2-BBC and 59.9 on LRS3-TED.
entries.condition: LRS2-BBC and LRS3-TED sentence-level benchmarks; outside-method results are copied from original papers unless otherwise stated.

entries.text: Table 2 reports Conv-Seq2Seq WER of 16.3 on LRW, 51.7 on LRS2-BBC, and 60.1 on LRS3-TED.
entries.condition: LRW word-level and LRS2-BBC/LRS3-TED sentence-level; outside-method results are copied from original papers unless otherwise stated.

entries.text: Ours-TC is reported to improve WER by 6.7 points over its Temporal Convolution baseline without the master.
entries.condition: LRW word-level; Ours-TC versus the corresponding Temporal Convolution baseline.
entries.quote: Ours-TC signiﬁcantly outperforms its baseline Tempo- ral Convolution which is without the master module, with a WER improvement of 6.7%.

entries.text: Ours-TM is reported as best on LRW and 2.0 WER points better than Conv-Seq2Seq.
entries.condition: LRW; Ours-TM 14.3 versus Conv-Seq2Seq 16.3 in Table 2.

entries.text: Against TM-Seq2Seq, Ours-TM is reported to improve WER by 0.6 points on LRS2-BBC and 0.9 on LRS3-TED, using less training data despite TM-Seq2Seq's extra non-public MV-LRS data.
entries.condition: LRS2-BBC: 49.2 vs 49.8; LRS3-TED: 59.0 vs 59.9. The authors state TM-Seq2Seq used extra non-public MV-LRS data.
entries.quote: our method achieves a better per- formance with WER improvements 0.6% on LRS2-BBC and 0.9% on LRS3-TED in the case of using much less training data.

entries.text: Against Conv-Seq2Seq, Ours-TM is reported to improve WER by 2.5 points on LRS2-BBC and 1.1 on LRS3-TED.
entries.condition: LRS2-BBC: 49.2 vs 51.7; LRS3-TED: 59.0 vs 60.1.

entries.text: On LRW's four highest-error cases, Ours-TC without KD has error rates of 74%, 70%, 70%, and 66%.
entries.condition: LRW top-four cases listed as THESE, THERE, THING, and UNDER; Table 3 compares Ours-TC w/o KD and Ours-TC.

entries.text: For the four selected LRW cases, the authors claim nearly 6% average accuracy improvement when multiple phonemes map to one viseme.
entries.condition: Top-four highest-error LRW cases; comparison of Ours-TC with Ours-TC w/o KD; described example phonemes TH and DH versus viseme /t/.

entries.text: On LRS2-BBC, the audio teacher reports WER of 17.2.
entries.condition: Table 4; audio and video modality teacher/student pairs; curriculum learning is not used for these comparisons.
entries.quote: Audio Teacher % 17.2

entries.text: On LRS2-BBC, the audio-visual teacher reports WER of 15.6.
entries.condition: Table 4; audio-visual teacher/student pair; curriculum learning is not used for these comparisons.

entries.text: On LRS2-BBC, the audio master reports WER of 19.1.
entries.condition: Table 4; audio master/student pair; curriculum learning is not used for these comparisons.

entries.text: On LRS2-BBC, the video master reports WER of 59.1.
entries.condition: Table 4; video master/student pair; curriculum learning is not used for these comparisons.

entries.text: On LRS2-BBC, the audio-visual master reports WER of 16.9.
entries.condition: Table 4; audio-visual master/student pair; curriculum learning is not used for these comparisons.

entries.text: The authors report that students learned from masters outperform those learned from teachers, while teacher networks can outperform their master counterparts.
entries.condition: LRS2-BBC Table 4; comparisons cover audio, video, and audio-visual variants, without curriculum learning.

entries.text: Table 5 reports baseline LRS2-BBC WER of 57.5 with AV:A:V weights 0:0:0.
entries.condition: Baseline AV:A:V weights 0:0:0; curriculum learning not used in this weight-setting comparison.

entries.text: Table 5 reports teacher weight setting T1 WER of 54.1 on LRS2-BBC.
entries.condition: T1 uses AV:A:V weights 1:0:0; curriculum learning not used in this weight-setting comparison.

entries.text: For the 2-layer TC setup, Table 6 reports Ours-TC WER of 19.8 without curriculum.
entries.condition: LRW-only training; 2-layer temporal-convolution backend; baseline B.-2 and Ours-TC; WER and training time as Table 6 reports.

entries.text: For the 8-layer TC setup, Table 6 reports Ours-TC WER of 14.0 without curriculum.
entries.condition: LRW-only training; 8-layer temporal-convolution backend; baseline B.-8 and Ours-TC; WER and training time as Table 6 reports.

entries.text: For the [18] backend, Table 6 reports Ours-TC WER of 11.9 without curriculum.
entries.condition: LRW-only training; the more advanced backend used in [18]; WER and training time as Table 6 reports.

entries.text: With curriculum, Table 6 reports baseline WERs 24.3, 17.0, and 14.7 and Ours-TC WERs 18.7, 13.5, and 11.8 for the corresponding backends.
entries.condition: LRW-only training; baseline systems; curriculum learning enabled.

entries.text: The authors say curriculum learning helps a lightweight model's performance and convergence, but gives less performance improvement with an advanced backend and mainly accelerates training.
entries.condition: LRW-only comparisons in Table 6; advanced backend is the one used in [18].
entries.quote: Nonetheless, when replacing with an advanced model, the improvement of CL degrades, and it mainly helps to accelerate the training.

entries.text: Training uses alternating student and master stages, a temporary student update, cross-entropy supervision, and dynamic fusion loss.
entries.condition: Student loss is cross entropy plus λs times dynamic fusion loss; master loss includes student feedback and three supervised master outputs, with λm weighting the master terms.
entries.quote: The train- ing objective contains two terms: cross entropy loss LCE and dynamic fusion loss LDF .

entries.text: The curriculum sorts paired samples using audio- and video-tutor confidence and grows the sample fraction by a fixed exponential pacing function.
entries.unit: initial fraction; pacing factor; iterations per step
entries.condition: Algorithm 1 curriculum parameters; training datasets are ranked by confidence before pacing is applied.
entries.quote: Gi = min(G0 × P ⌊i ξ ⌋, 1), i > 0,

entries.text: Pretraining learning rate is 1e-3.
entries.condition: Pretraining stage.

entries.text: The word-level configurations use temporal-convolution backends; sentence-level configurations use transformer Seq2Seq and predict characters.
entries.condition: TC is also used for word-level pretraining; the sentence-level model replaces TC with TM-Seq2Seq before fine-tuning.

entries.text: The visual frontend replaces its initial 2D convolution with a 3D convolution using a 5×7×7 kernel.
entries.condition: Visual stream; audio first-convolution filter is 5ms with stride 0.25ms; audio frontend uses ResNet-18.

entries.text: The audio stream consumes raw waveform; transformer Seq2Seq uses multi-head attention and feedforward blocks, and audio/video features are concatenated for the joint classifier.
entries.condition: Joint audio-visual combination is master-only; model variants use temporal convolution or transformer Seq2Seq backends.

entries.text: The output is a directly recognized word class for word-level tasks or a character sequence for sentence-level tasks.
entries.condition: Silent lip video is the student's input; sentence prediction is character-by-character.

entries.text: The authors identify inherent visual ambiguity: different phonemes such as p and b may share a similar lip shape and be hard to distinguish from video.
entries.condition: Motivation for audio knowledge transfer; this is described as a limitation of visual information.

entries.text: The authors state that cross-modal domain gap can create learning ambiguity and limit lip-reading performance.
entries.condition: Audio-to-video knowledge transfer; the issue motivates the bimodal master and dynamic fusion design.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge that teacher networks can have better standalone performance than corresponding masters.
entries.condition: Table 4 modality comparisons on LRS2-BBC; curriculum learning is not used.
entries.quote: No matter which modality is used, the teachers always per- form better than their counterpart masters.

entries.text: Simple concatenation-based cross-modal fusion is described as yielding only limited improvement, motivating the dynamic fusion module.
entries.condition: The authors refer to Table 4 teacher/student modality comparisons.

entries.text: The exact test partition, test-set sample count, and partition-specific evaluation protocol are not reported for each table result.
entries.condition: Datasets and aggregate WER comparisons are named, but Table 1-6 do not identify exact test-subset sizes or sample counts for the reported scores.

entries.text: The paper does not report random seeds, repeated-run counts, variance, or confidence intervals for the experiments.
entries.condition: Applies to reported WER and training-time comparisons throughout the experiments.
entries.quote: The student and the master are trained alternatively using SGD optimizer with a momen- tum of 0.9 and a weight decay of 1e-4.

entries.text: Speaker/subject overlap across training, validation, and test partitions, speaker counts, and any session-level split constraints are not stated.
entries.condition: The paper names benchmark partitions but does not specify speaker-disjointness, speaker counts, or session overlap for evaluation.

entries.text: Exact checkpoint/model-selection criteria and validation-subset definition are not supplied; the paper only states that validation data are used for master updates and learning-rate plateau decisions.
entries.condition: The master update uses different samples and a validation set instead of a training set; fine-tuning uses the related train-val set, but exact selection protocol is not detailed.
entries.quote: Because when up- dating the master, the student should utilize a validation set instead of a training set.

entries.text: Pixel-intensity normalization and audio waveform normalization are not specified; the paper only describes geometric face transformation and raw-wave input.
entries.condition: No mean/std, intensity scaling, waveform amplitude normalization, or equivalent normalization parameters are given.

entries.text: No chance-level or majority-class baseline is reported for the word-level or sentence-level tasks.
entries.condition: Vocabulary sizes are provided (500 word classes and 40 sentence symbols), but chance performance is not stated.

entries.text: Inference decoding settings such as beam width, search procedure, and decoding constraints are not reported.
entries.condition: Sentence-level backend is described as transformer Seq2Seq, but no inference-time decoding configuration is given.

entries.text: The paper does not state whether an external language model or other use-time aid is used, nor provide an LM configuration.
entries.condition: The described student is visual-input-only; any language-model rescoring or additional inference aid is not specified.
entries.quote: The student takes XV as input, and outputs probabilites fs(XV ; θs).

entries.text: Comparative baseline results are mostly copied from prior papers, and the paper does not establish a uniform reimplementation or matched-data evaluation protocol for every baseline.
entries.condition: The authors say results are copied from original papers unless stated otherwise; training data and protocol may differ, including the explicitly noted extra non-public MV-LRS data for TM-Seq2Seq.

entries.text: No real-time, field, cross-device, or deployment evaluation is reported; applications are proposed as motivation rather than tested use cases.
entries.condition: Benchmark experiments only; no latency, runtime-at-inference, device, user, or operational evaluation is described.

entries.text: Each LRW video is described as 1.16 seconds long and 29 frames.
entries.condition: LRW dataset description, not a test-subset specification.

entries.text: LRS2-BBC is described as including 143,000 utterances and 2.3 million words.
entries.condition: Dataset-level totals, not test-subset sample counts.

entries.text: LRS3-TED is described as including 150,000 utterances and over 4.2 million words.
entries.condition: Dataset-level totals, not test-subset sample counts.

entries.condition: LRS2-BBC and LRS3-TED; special tokens are SPACE, PAD, EOS, and punctuation mark.

entries.text: Pretraining uses a word-level temporal-convolution backend with LRW and the LRS2-BBS/LRS3-TED pretrain sets.
entries.condition: The paper spells LRS2-BBS in this training-protocol sentence; dataset section and other passages call it LRS2-BBC.

entries.text: Word-level models are fine-tuned on LRW; sentence-level models replace TC with TM-Seq2Seq, continue pretraining on the corresponding sentence-corpus pretrain set, and fine-tune on the related train-val set.
entries.condition: LRW for word-level; LRS2-BBC or LRS3-TED for the sentence-level path.

entries.text: Training follows Afouras et al. for data augmentation and audio-subtitle forced alignment.
entries.condition: The proposed curriculum learning is applied alongside those strategies.

entries.text: Training alternates two stages: student training and master training.
entries.condition: Student stage trains the student; master stage uses a temporary student update and feedback to update the master.

entries.text: The authors introduce dynamic fusion loss to balance and fuse knowledge from the audio, video, and combined streams.
entries.condition: Used as regularization during student training, with modality weights guided by audio/video tutor features.

entries.text: The authors claim Ours-TM performs best on both sentence-level benchmarks.
entries.condition: LRS2-BBC and LRS3-TED; comparison in Table 2.

entries.text: The authors report that dynamically weighted master fusion setting M4 gives the best result among the Table 5 weight settings.
entries.condition: LRS2-BBC WER; M4 uses AV weight 1 and dynamically weighted audio/video terms wa and wv; curriculum learning not used.

entries.text: The audio frontend uses ResNet-18; its initial convolution uses a 5ms filter and 0.25ms stride for waveform input.
entries.condition: Audio stream processes raw waveform using 1D filters.

entries.text: Meta Pseudo Labels adapts the teacher from the student's performance on labelled data (general ML, image classification).
entries.condition: Abstract read (arXiv 2003.10580 v1, 2020-03).
entries.quote: the teacher in Meta Pseudo Labels is constantly adapted by the feedback of the student's performance

entries.text: Learning to Teach optimizes a teacher model from student feedback by reinforcement learning (general ML).
entries.condition: Abstract read (ICLR 2018).
entries.quote: The teacher model leverages the feedback from the student model to optimize its own teaching strategies

entries.text: Table 6 trains on LRW only, the same setting as the [18] backend it borrows.
entries.condition: LRW-only training; backends: 2 TC layers, 8 TC layers, and the backend of [18] (Lipreading using temporal convolutional networks).
entries.quote: Note that here we only use LRW as training data, which is the same training setting as in [18].

entries.text: The authors state that previous lip-reading methods [1, 7, 27] sample training data randomly and ignore sample order.
entries.condition: [1] Afouras et al. 2018 (Deep AVSR), [7] Chung et al. 2017 (LRS), [27] Zhang et al. 2019 (Conv-Seq2Seq).
entries.quote: Previous lip reading methods [1, 7, 27] are proposed to randomly sample training data

entries.text: The curriculum is presented as based on the cited curriculum-learning works [4, 13].
entries.condition: [4] Bengio et al. 2009; [13] Hacohen and Weinshall 2019.

entries.text: The authors say collaborative (online) distillation transfers knowledge between students without considering each student's feedback.
entries.condition: Related work on DML, ONE, CLNN, KDCL.
entries.quote: rative distillation methods transfer knowledge between stu- dents without considering the feedback of each student.

entries.text: The authors contrast their trainable master with most existing methods, which distill from a pretrained teacher.
entries.condition: Contribution list.

entries.text: The authors observe in Table 1 that a video teacher also improves the video student.
entries.condition: LRS2-BBC; video teacher of the same structure as the student.

entries.text: Table 1 teachers share one structure and differ only in the modality they were pretrained on; the students are also identical.
entries.condition: LRS2-BBC.
entries.quote: to test the impact of the teachers which share a same structure but pretrained on different modalities.

entries.text: Table 2 does not list [18] (temporal convolutional networks), whose backend the paper uses in Table 6, nor any distillation-based LRW system other than its own.
entries.condition: Table 2 compares MT, Tem. Conv., WAS, Bi-LSTM, TM-CTC, TM-Seq2Seq, Conv-Seq2Seq, LIBS, TM-CTC-KD.

entries.text: Afouras et al. decode with a 6-gram language model and an 8192-width beam.
entries.condition: LRS2 and LRS3 results of the KD study.

entries.text: The best Afouras et al. results are 51.3% WER on LRS2 and 59.8% on LRS3, after unsupervised pre-training on extra data and full supervision.

entries.quote: Finally, training on each dataset with full supervision after unsupervised pre-training, yields the best results, 51.3% for LRS2 and 59.8% for LRS3.

entries.text: Afouras et al. name cross-modal ASR distillation into an audio-visual recognizer (Wei Li et al.) as the closest work.
entries.condition: Teacher: ASR; student: audio-visual recognizer.
entries.quote: The closest work to ours is Wei et al. [31] who apply cross-modal distillation from ASR for learning audio-visual speech recognition.

entries.text: LIBS assumes a given pre-trained speech recognizer and distils it into the lip reader.

entries.quote: a pre-trained speech recognizer is given, and attempt to distill knowledge concealed in the speech recognizer to the target lip reader

entries.text: LIBS reports 45.53% CER and 65.29% WER on LRS2.

entries.text: Xiao et al. train two video branches jointly with a bidirectional distillation loss so that each learns from the other.

entries.quote: we make the two streams learn from each other in the learning process by introducing a bidirectional knowledge distillation loss to train the two branches jointly.

questions.q: Does the evaluated student require audio at use time?
questions.answer: The described student takes video as input, while audio is supplied to the master/audio tutor during training. The paper does not give a separate deployment evaluation.

questions.q: What results support the claimed benchmark superiority?
questions.answer: The paper reports Ours-TM WER of 14.3 on LRW, 49.2 on LRS2-BBC, and 59.0 on LRS3-TED, and compares against the cited baselines in Table 2.

questions.q: Can the reported evaluation conditions be fully reconstructed from the paper?
questions.answer: Not fully: exact test-subset sizes, random seeds/repetitions, speaker/session overlap, precise validation/model-selection details, normalization, chance baselines, and decoding/LM settings are not reported.

questions.q: Triage: does the evaluator's population critique hold?
questions.answer: Yes: prior rows included perception, neuroimaging and non-decoder studies and duplicate versions; rebuilt with tools/exclude_reading.json (prior 167).
